verdict.reasoning: The clinician opens with: "You've mentioned on our notes that you're suffering from bad diarrhea."

Duration and frequency are stated: "It's been happening for about three days now" and "Four to five [times a day]." Consistency is discussed as variable between watery and loose: "It probably depends on the time of day, to be honest" in response to watery vs loose stools.
Patient states: "it's pretty standard diarrhea where there's like a little bit of abdominal pain." This supports mild abdominal pain.
Patient says: "I threw up once."
Patient notes: "A little bit of appetite loss, I guess, versus the normal."
When asked about drinking, patient confirms: "Yeah, yeah, yeah" and clinician comments "you're still drinking plenty," indicating adequate fluid intake.
In response to fever: "Maybe a little bit, but it hasn't been that in particular hasn't been too worrying," which indicates a possible low‑grade fever.
On blood and mucus: "No blood" and after mucus explanation: "No, no."
Patient says: "nothing funky in my diet or no travels recently," supporting no recent travel or clear dietary trigger.
Patient reports: "I. Probably at asthma or. Or, I don't know, I guess I still have it."

Patient says the inhaler is "Lexapro" and that it is "Yellow." However, Lexapro is an antidepressant, not an inhaler. The clinician responds "Not heard of it… I'll have to check that one," indicating uncertainty. Claiming it as a definite "yellow Lexapro inhaler" is not supported and conflicts with standard use of Lexapro.
When asked about allergies, patient replies: "Nothing. Yeah, nothing." and clinician confirms "No allergies at all."
Patient states: "My dad had hypertension." and then "Has hypertension? Yeah. Hypertension."
Patient says: "He died of bowel cancer 10 years ago." and when asked age: "62."
The transcript contains no discussion of social history (e.g., occupation, smoking, alcohol, living situation), so stating it was not discussed is consistent with the absence of such content.
Clinician notes: "you're still drinking plenty and you look like you're not dehydrated, which is a good sign," implying on visual assessment the patient appears well hydrated.

The clinician describes frequency, hydration, and when to worry, but does not explicitly state the diagnosis as "acute self-limited diarrhoea" or "suspected viral gastroenteritis" nor explicitly say "no red-flag features." This is inferred, not stated.
Asthma is mentioned in history and inhaler queried, but there is no explicit assessment that asthma is currently stable.

Clinician advises: "you could get something called Di Rolite over the counter. So it helps to replenish the salts that you've been... lost through going to the toilet," which corresponds to an oral rehydration solution as needed.
Clinician recommends a soft diet: "that will be like crackers, toast, jam" and later "you can start off with some just boiled vegetables and mash."

Diet advice: "avoid dairy, fish, meat, eggs while you're having the diarrhea" and later: "Once you're okay with that for about 48 hours, then you can start having meat" and "Milk is not a good idea. Yogurts are a good idea." This supports avoiding dairy except yogurt, and avoiding meat/egg/fish until 48 hours after tolerating soft foods (i.e., effectively symptom-free/tolerating diet).
Clinician says: "if your diarrhea doesn't go away in a week's time… We need a stool sample," implying the patient should re-contact/seek care if it lasts more than one week.

Clinician advises: "When we start worrying about diarrhea is if you're going more than eight times a day" and later: "if you're going about six to eight times a day, that means there's a high chance that you are having dehydration and you might need to go into hospital at that point... If that happens, do get in touch with us again."

Clinician states: "if you're passing blood. We need a stool sample" indicating need to seek further care if blood (a red flag) appears. Mucus is similarly discussed as a red-flag feature earlier; the plan implies return if such concerning features appear.
Fever is asked about but there is no explicit advice: "return if fever increases" or similar wording in the plan.

Clinician links high frequency with dehydration and potential hospital: "if you're going about six to eight times a day, that means there's a high chance that you are having dehydration and you might need to go into hospital at that point in time. If that happens, do get in touch with us again." This ties dehydration concern to further evaluation; stool sample was mentioned earlier for persistent diarrhea or blood.
There is no explicit instruction regarding asthma management or to "continue the current inhaler" in the plan.

Clinician says: "All this is all recorded in your app, so you can go back. I'll put that all in detail. So... you can go back and read the notes." This advises the patient to review recorded instructions in the app.
